description: We are a passionate team of Computer Engineering students developing an interactive planetary exploration platform powered by NASA's open data. Our project enables users to explore Earth, Mars, and the Moon through 3D terrain visualization, elevation analysis, slope calculations, and intelligent pathfinding. We combine programming, simulation, and scientific innovation to create an engaging experience. We welcome creative minds skilled in AI, 3D development, GIS, and data analysis.
summary:
We built Planetary Analog Lab to find places on Earth where researchers could practice for missions to the Moon or Mars. One of the things you can do in the app is put part of Jezero crater on Mars next to a place like Wadi Rum in Jordan and run the same route test on both in 3D. If you lower the slope limit, a route that worked a second ago might have to go around a hill. Sometimes there’s no way through at all.

The app uses NASA elevation data to find Earth sites worth comparing in the first place. It looks at areas of the same size and ranks the sites in our dataset by how similar their slopes, roughness and changes in height are. You can see what each site has in common with the area you picked and then try the route test for yourself. The idea is to give researchers a better sense of where to go for a field test and what they could try once they get there.
details:
We built Planetary Analog Lab to help researchers find places on Earth where they could test ideas for Moon and Mars missions. You can pick a location on the globe or enter its coordinates, then choose a 1 × 1, 5 × 5 or 10 × 10 km area. The app compares it with areas of the same size in our Earth dataset. We used NASADEM for Earth, MOLA and HiRISE for Mars, and LOLA and SLDEM2015 for the Moon. The app measures slope, roughness and elevation changes and shows why each Earth site ranked where it did.

The part we were most interested in was what happens when you try to cross both sites. In the 3D view, you can pick a start and an end point and try three routes. One looks for the shortest route within the slope limit, one favors gentler slopes and one uses terrain costs you can adjust. You can see the distance, how much the route climbs and the steepest section along the way. If the app can’t find a route under the limit you set, it shows that too.

We ran the same set of route tests on both areas and checked how often a route was possible and how its length changed at different slope limits. We used those results in the ranking. In one test, an Earth site went from seventh to third after we added the route results.

We built the interface and browser tools with JavaScript and used WebGL for the interactive globes. We also used Python and FastAPI for the terrain analysis backend. Since the data comes at different resolutions, we added a way to repeat a comparison on a coarser grid and see how much the results change. The app can export a report with the sources, settings and results.

The goal is to make it easier for researchers to decide which sites are worth visiting and what to check once they get there. Soil conditions and how a real rover handles the ground would still need to be tested in the field.
